text: Wednesday morning on the rooftop, Nib eats cereal with no mask on. Nobody ever comes up here.
Then someone pounds on the stair door.
Nib slaps on his mask and freezes, spoon in his mouth. Jaeha spits out his toothpaste.
It's Choi, with breakfast and an agenda. Jaeha welcomes him in with toothpaste still on his lip.
Choi stops dead. Across the roof, the husk sits frozen, milk dripping from its chin, and Jaeha smiles much too hard.
Choi lays out the kimbap and his incident report. The husk's eyes never leave the kimbap.
Choi needs a killer for that boss. Jaeha's answer is polite, flattering, and useless.
Then there's the missing fortune. Jaeha's next answer is technically true.
Choi reaches for the kimbap. Empty foil, and the husk's cheek is bulging.
Choi turns slowly toward the husk. Jaeha has a new adjective ready.
Then the smirk goes. Off the record, rich strangers are curious about the gate's survivors, and Mok is trashing Jaeha's name.
For a second the polite mask slips. Jaeha knows exactly what that kind of interest means.
At the door, Choi warns him about Mok. Jaeha's reply is the truest thing he's said all morning.
Choi tosses a last roll over his shoulder, and the husk catches it blind. Choi returns Jaeha's own line.
His notebook has a page on Mok's crew: who they are, how they work, what they smoke.
His next job is an easy survey, his name on the public board. He's counting on Mok reading it.
That afternoon, they ride a dead escalator into an arcade where every shutter is down.
The survey officer hands over the chalk without looking up. His concern is purely administrative.
Yerin has appointed herself the medic. Jaeha swears it's perfectly safe, for a man expecting a trap.
By the gate: a fresh cigarette butt with a thin green band, and a boot print pointing in.
Jaeha's eyes narrow. A menthol.
Inside, a ruined granary of giant stone silos. Among friends, Nib stops pretending to be a husk.
At a dark doorway, Nib steps aside, palm out. Jaeha objects on behalf of husks everywhere. Nib wins.
Eyes closed, Jaeha rides Link up the stairs, forty metres of a possible hundred and sixty.
A chalk X, ten thousand won, and Nib steps neatly round it.
Nib hangs upside down from a beam to point out a pit. Yerin has never been this excited about a pit.
Then a round chamber: two ceiling chutes, a lever on a high ledge. Jaeha stops Yerin with one arm.
Through Nib's eyes: an old plate under clean grain, and a modern zip tie holding a chute's catch open.
Jaeha whispers his reasoning: two things in this room are new, and the gate didn't put them there.
Yerin goes pale: she knows who this trap was for. Jaeha's answer is the cigarette from the gate.
So he turns their habit against them. Whoever sets a trap comes back to look at the catch.
He peels off the orange vest he's known by. Yerin doesn't like where this is going.
Nib shoves a stone block off the ledge onto the plate.
The chute bangs open, and the trap meant for Jaeha buries the plate in grain.
When the dust settles, his vest lies on the mound, an empty glove poking out like a hand.
Up on the ledge, by the second lever, they hide and wait. Yerin has opinions. Jaeha watches the door.
It doesn't take the hour. Nib's notched ear twitches.
Two Black Hound men stroll in: the bald shield-bearer from Mok's back room, and a wiry trapper smoking a menthol.
The trapper thinks it's funny. The shield-bearer has orders, and one of them is about a phone.
A menthol butt lands beside the empty glove. Same brand.
Then, to make sure, the shield-bearer drives his sword down through the T on the vest.
Yerin clamps her hands over her mouth. Jaeha doesn't move, eyes cold.
Then they kneel to dig for the body and the phone, right under the second chute.
The notebook snaps shut.
Jaeha and Nib haul the lever down together.
And a torrent of grain buries them both.
When the dust clears, they're buried to the armpits, coughing, and going nowhere.
Jaeha leans over the rail with his phone recording and his best customer-service voice.
But the trapper wrenches one arm free, and there's a loaded hand crossbow in it.
Jaeha doesn't flinch. He points one finger at the ceiling, polite as a tour guide.
A cracked hatch trembles over the trapper, trickling grain onto his head.
He drops the crossbow.
Then the questions, phone still recording. The shield-bearer cracks first: Mok suspects the back-room recording.
Jaeha calls it in, bowing to his phone like a citizen reporting a lost umbrella.
On the way out, Yerin asks about that cracked hatch. His answer is honest, at least.
At dusk, officers haul the grain-covered pair up to the street, where Bomi is waiting.
The survey pays a hundred and fifty thousand won, still a little short of the rent.
Bomi is delighted by the state of Mok's men. Jaeha offers a correction instead of an explanation.
Then she shows him her phone: the sewer frame. She wants him to know she's sitting on it.
Jaeha's smile freezes. Behind him, the husk's eye slides toward the phone.
Then the grin drops. For once she isn't performing: she wants the truth, and the restaurant is running out of time.
Jaeha drops his act too. He counts out two terms and sweetens the deal with a promise.
Bomi pumps his hand before he changes his mind. The one the deal is about gets no vote.
Bomi squishes Nib's cheeks with star-struck eyes, and he radiates pure murder.
Across the street, a man in a very nice suit, earpiece in, silver hexagon pin, lowers a long-lens camera.
That night, Jaeha stuffs the slashed vest deep into the laundry basket. Seoa has her headphones on.
But grain is trickling out of the pocket.
Seoa holds it up, a finger through the sword slash. She doesn't shout this time.
He can't find the polite smile or meet her eyes. So he makes the same promise again.
Seoa doesn't blink. She has heard those exact words before, from someone else.
A memory, at a child's height: their father at the door with his lunch bag, the sky outside turning red.
